nameStory: The 'two-lobed' part of this tiny plant's name comes from its distinctive leaves, which are split into two rounded sections like a pair of miniature green ears. 'Flapwort' refers to how these leaf lobes can fold and flap slightly in the breeze, plus the old English suffix '-wort' meaning plant.
description: Two-lobed Flapwort is a tiny liverwort - a primitive, moss-like plant that's one of the simplest land plants on Earth. It forms small, flat patches or cushions that hug tightly to rock surfaces, rarely growing more than a few millimeters tall. Each individual plant looks like a series of small, split leaves pressed flat against the surface, creating intricate green carpets that you'll need to look closely to appreciate.

idTips.label: Split leaves
idTips.description: Each tiny leaf is deeply divided into two rounded lobes that feel soft and slightly fleshy when gently touched with a fingertip

idTips.label: Flat growth pattern
idTips.description: Plants lie completely flat against rock surfaces like green paint, with no upright stems or branches reaching skyward

idTips.label: Rock attachment
idTips.description: Firmly adhered to bare rock faces and feels almost rubbery when you try to peel it off gently

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches are typically smaller than a quarter, though several may grow together to form larger colonies

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Fresh specimens are bright green, becoming brownish or blackish when dry, with a slightly glossy surface

habitat: Look for Two-lobed Flapwort on exposed rock faces, particularly granite outcrops and stone walls in shaded or partially shaded areas. It prefers slightly acidic rocks that stay moist but not waterlogged, often growing alongside other small liverworts and mosses. In New England, it's most likely found in rocky areas of forests and along stone walls in rural areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth appears bright green and fresh-looking as moisture returns. This is the best time to see the characteristic two-lobed leaves clearly.
seasonality.summer: May appear somewhat dried and darker during hot, dry periods, but revives quickly after rain showers.
seasonality.fall: Often looks its best in the cool, moist conditions of autumn, with vibrant green coloration returning.
seasonality.winter: Survives under snow cover and can be found year-round, though it may appear brownish or blackened when frozen.

funFact: **Note: This identification guide is based on limited training data - with only one recorded observation in New England, this species may be extremely rare or the identification uncertain.** Like other liverworts, this ancient plant can completely dry out and appear dead for months, then spring back to vibrant green life within minutes of getting wet!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, flat liverworts on rocks, but the consistently two-lobed leaf structure sets it apart from species with simple, undivided leaves or those with more complex branching patterns.
contextualKnowledge: Liverworts like this one are among Earth's most ancient land plants, virtually unchanged for over 400 million years. The name 'liverwort' comes from medieval times when people thought the lobed leaves resembled the shape of a liver and might cure liver ailments.
compareHints: Since this appears to be the only Nardia species commonly found in New England, compare it with other small rock-dwelling liverworts in the region. Unlike many other liverworts that have simple, unlobed leaves or complex branching, Two-lobed Flapwort consistently shows that distinctive split-leaf pattern that gives it its name.
